title: Olfactory bulb-cortex oscillations encode perceived odor intensity rather than concentration
experiments_summary: The study used the electrobulbogram (EBG), an EEG-based noninvasive method, to simultaneously record oscillatory activity from the olfactory bulb (OB) and piriform cortex (PC) in 46 human participants during odor presentation. Three neutral odors from different chemical classes (n-Butanol, Undecanal, 5-Nonanone) were each presented at two concentrations (Low and High) plus a clean air condition, delivered binasally for 2 seconds via a sniff-triggered olfactometer. Participants rated perceived intensity and pleasantness on visual analogue scales after each trial. EEG/EBG signals (64 + 4 electrodes) were source-reconstructed using eLORETA with individual structural MRI-based finite element head models, constraining analysis to OB and PC ROIs, plus control regions (primary visual cortex V1 and posterior cingulate cortex PCC). Time-frequency power spectra were computed using the Superlet method. Linear mixed-effects models were applied at each time-frequency point to assess relationships between spectral power and either odor concentration or perceived intensity, controlling for valence and sniff parameters, with cluster-based permutation testing (1,000 permutations, weighted cluster-mass correction). A principal components analysis (PCA) was also performed on raw OB signals to examine concentration effects outside the time-frequency domain. Odor vapor-phase concentrations were independently measured using proton transfer reaction time-of-flight mass spectrometry (PTR-TOF), and analyses were repeated using a continuous effective concentration metric. OB-PC functional connectivity was assessed via coherence spectra computed with the Superlet method. A Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier with leave-one-out cross-validation was applied in a binned searchlight manner to the coherence spectrogram to decode concentration and perceived intensity, with significance evaluated using Monte-Carlo permutation testing and weighted cluster-mass correction. Effective (directional) connectivity was assessed using spectral Granger causality with multi-tapered FFT and DPSS frequency smoothing, contrasting OB-to-PC versus PC-to-OB directions. Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) between beta phase and gamma amplitude was evaluated using the Tort modulation index algorithm in time windows identified by coherence and Granger analyses, with significance tested via linear mixed-effects models and Monte-Carlo permutation correction. Single-trial burst analysis was performed by identifying oscillatory events in the beta (12-30 Hz) and gamma (30-100 Hz) bands exceeding 1 SD above a 10-trial mean and lasting at least three cycles, then relating burst rates to concentration and perceived intensity using linear mixed-effects models with Box-Cox transformation of the response variable and Monte-Carlo permutation testing.
